latin.312: GAR. Quinto quaeritur. Si primus actus peccandi fuit actus naturae, cur non & primus actus generandi, ut in Adamo dicamur Cainum, aut Sethum genitos esse? Resp. Mitto viri docti paralogismum, Sethi genituram primo actui, quo Adamus generavit, attribuenti, qui tamen nonnisi tertius esse potuit, Gen. 4. PLAC. Quale, quaeso, est hoc paralogismum? Vereor ne id potius Viro docto tribui debeat, qui animadvertisse non videtur vim disjunctionis qua usus fueram; nempe duplex fuit actus generandi Adami, unus absolute primus, alter primus in genere eorum unde orti sumus.
latin.313: Ille fuit actus quo Cainum genuit, hic quo Sethum: Ex Setho enim, non vero ex Caino, nos omnes originem ducimus: utrumque, ne quod pateret effugium, complexus sum. GAR. Ad rem ipsam dico, non quemlibet primum actum naturae fuisse posteris imputandum (hoc enim Scriptura neque aperte testatur, neque vel levissime insinuat) sed primum tantum actum naturae deficientis ab ea perfectione, quam ipsi Deus creatione indiderat, eaque mutata comminationem, quo die primum de fructu vetito comederis, moriendo morieris. Cum igitur primus actus generandi, nullus fuerit per se actus naturae rebellantis ac deficientis a creatore, magis quam primus actus respirandi, concoquendi, ambulandi, &c. Sed prima illa inobedientia fuerit primus deficientis naturae actus, quo scilicet Adamus a primario foedere defecit turpissime, nemo mirari debet, si & primus peccandi actus posteris imputetur, & primus generandi actus non imputetur.
latin.314: PLAC. Non igitur imputatur nobis inobedientia illa Adami, qua est actus Adami: alii enim multi eius actus non imputantur: nec qua est primus eius actus, non enim absolute primus fuit, sed tantum in suo genere, nec qua est in suo genere primus actus naturae; hoc enim aliis quoque actibus convenit, sed qua est actus naturae deficientis. Iam hoc quaeritur, quare actus naturae deficientis nobis potius imputari debeat, quam actus naturae non deficientis? id enim, ut video, a defectione est naturae, non ab ipsa natura. Quid est enim cur, cum caetera sunt paria, malum potius nobis imputetur, quam bonum?
latin.315: Nam si peccare sequitur esse, ut certe debet (non entis enim non sunt accidentia) actus generandi is est cuius vi primum sumus, hunc sequi debere videtur, & in eo fundari is actus cuius vi primum peccatores sumus; saltem hic nos non facit peccatores, nisi illo mediante: itaque illum praesupponit: peccare enim praesupponit esse, & prius est naturae ordine nos fieri, quam fieri peccatores. Si ergo fuimus peccatores imputatione alieni peccati quae fit nostrum, ea imputatio sequi debet aliquid quo fuimus homines, siquidem ordine naturae prius sumus homines quam peccatores, prius est subjectum quam eius accidens.
latin.316: Is autem actus, quo primo facti sumus homines, est actus ille generandi, quo Adamus Sethum genuit: quare imputatio peccati primi antecedens seu immediata supponit illum actum. Prius igitur fuit nos haberi pro genitis ab Adamo, quam pro peccatoribus, & primus ille actus quo geniti sumus prius ad nos pertinuit, quam ille quo facti sumus peccatores. Imputatur enim nobis peccatum Adae, quia sumus eius posteri: sumus autem eius posteri, quia nos genuit: nos autem genuit, quatenus genuit Sethum. Actus ergo quo genuit Sethum ordine naturae antecedit imputationem peccati. Sed tamen, si viro docto fides habetur, imputatum est nobis peccatum Adami diu antequam Sethum genuisset, illo ipso tempore quo commissum est: aut igitur antecessit etiam fieri Adami.
latin.317: GAR. Quaeritur sexto. Si ut Christi justitia nobis imputatur, ita & peccatum Adae nostrum sit imputatione, cur non, ut Christus dicitur justitia nostra, ita & Adamus dicitur peccatum nostrum? Resp. 1. Deum loqui ut vult; nostrum esse iis phrasibus esse contentos, quae in Scripturis occurrunt, quaeque Dei mentem, quantum salutis nostrae interest, satis evidenter exponunt. Quanquam ergo non dicit Scriptura Adamum esse peccatum nostrum; eas tamen locutiones adhibet, quae imputationem manifeste designant, de quo fuse dictum est antea. PLAC. Hac ratione seu interrogatione usum esse me non memini, nec cuius sit novi: sive tamen mea, aut alterius sit, accommodata fuisse videtur ad refellendam majorem argumenti, quo solet imputatio immediata maxime niti, Quemadmodum constituimur justi per Christum, eodem modo constituti sumus peccatores per Adamum: ostendit enim inter Christum & Adamum memorabile discrimen.

pass_a.312: Fifth erotema: if the first sin-act was an act of nature, why not the first generative act—so we are Cain or Seth in Adam? GAR brushes aside as paralogism tying Seth's birth to Adam's absolute first generative act (Gen. 4: that was at best third). Placeus flips the charge: the Learned Man missed the disjunction—Adam's generating is twofold: absolutely first, and first in the line from which we spring.
pass_a.313: Placeus fills the disjunction: Cain's begetting vs Seth's—we come from Seth, not Cain—and he covered both so no escape route remains. GAR then states the substance: Scripture never charges every first natural act to posterity, only the first act of a nature fallen from the perfection God gave in creation, under the death-threat for eating the forbidden fruit. Generating, like breathing, digesting, or walking, is not itself rebellion against the Creator; that first disobedience is the first failing-nature act and basest breach of the primary covenant—hence the first sin-act is charged to posterity, and the first generative act is not.
pass_a.314: Placeus: Adam's disobedience is not ours merely as his act (many of his acts are not charged), nor as absolutely first (only first in kind), nor as first-of-nature in kind (other acts share that), but as an act of failing nature. Then why charge failing-nature acts rather than non-failing ones? That hangs on the defect, not on nature as such—and with all else equal, why impute evil to us rather than good?
pass_a.315: If sinning follows being (non-beings have no accidents), the generative act is how we first are, and the act that first makes us sinners should follow and rest on it; at least it cannot make us sinners except through that prior act. Sinning presupposes being; in nature's order we become before we become sinners. So if we are sinners by another's imputed sin made ours, that imputation must follow something by which we were already human—subject before accident.
pass_a.316: The act that first made us human is Adam's begetting of Seth; so antecedent/immediate first-sin imputation presupposes it. We count as Adam's offspring before we count as sinners; we are posterity because he begot us, and he begot us as he begot Seth. Seth's begetting precedes sin-imputation in nature's order. Yet on the Learned Man's view the sin was charged at the moment of commission—long before Seth—so either imputation also ran ahead of Adam's own coming-to-be. Tip closes Q5.
pass_a.317: Sixth erotema opens: if Adam's sin is ours by imputation as Christ's righteousness is, why is Adam not called our sin as Christ is called our righteousness? GAR: take Scripture's phrases as God gave them; they mark imputation without that title. Placeus: he does not recall owning the question, but it fits to break the major that leans on a strict Christ/Adam same-mode parallel for constituting sinners and righteous. Natural tip into Q6 replies.

312: GAR. Fifth it is asked. If the first act of sinning was an act of nature, why not also the first act of generating, so that in Adam we should be said to have been begotten as Cain, or as Seth? Reply. I pass over the learned man's paralogism, which ascribes Seth's begetting to the first act by which Adam generated, though that could only have been the third, Gen. 4. PLAC. What, I ask, is this paralogism? I fear it rather belongs to the Learned Man, who does not seem to have noticed the force of the disjunction I had used; namely there was a twofold act of Adam's generating: one absolutely first, the other first in the kind of those from whom we spring.
313: That was the act by which he begot Cain, this by which he begot Seth: for from Seth, not from Cain, we all draw our origin: I embraced both, lest any escape should lie open. GAR. To the matter itself I say: not every first act of nature was to be imputed to posterity (for Scripture neither openly testifies this, nor even lightly hints it) but only the first act of a nature failing from that perfection which God had given it in creation, and with the threat changed: in the day you first eat of the forbidden fruit, dying you shall die. Since therefore the first act of generating was in itself no act of a nature rebelling and failing from the Creator, any more than the first act of breathing, digesting, walking, &c.; but that first disobedience was the first act of a failing nature, whereby Adam most basely fell from the primary covenant—no one ought to wonder if both the first act of sinning is imputed to posterity, and the first act of generating is not.
314: PLAC. Therefore that disobedience of Adam is not imputed to us insofar as it is an act of Adam: for many other acts of his are not imputed; nor insofar as it is his first act—for it was not absolutely first, but only first in its kind; nor insofar as it is in its kind the first act of nature—for that also fits other acts; but insofar as it is an act of a failing nature. Now this is asked: why ought an act of a failing nature rather be imputed to us than an act of a nature not failing? For that, as I see, is from the failing of nature, not from nature itself. For what reason, when the rest are equal, should evil rather be imputed to us than good?
315: For if sinning follows being, as it certainly ought (for of what is not there are no accidents), the act of generating is that by whose force we first are; this ought to seem to follow, and in it to be founded that act by whose force we first are sinners; at least this does not make us sinners except by means of that: and so it presupposes it: for to sin presupposes to be, and prior in the order of nature is that we become than that we become sinners. If therefore we were sinners by imputation of another's sin which becomes ours, that imputation ought to follow something by which we were humans, seeing that in nature's order we are humans before we are sinners, and the subject is prior to its accident.
316: But that act by which we were first made humans is that act of generating by which Adam begot Seth: therefore the antecedent or immediate imputation of the first sin presupposes that act. Earlier, then, was it that we be counted as begotten from Adam than as sinners, and that first act by which we were begotten belonged to us earlier than that by which we were made sinners. For Adam's sin is imputed to us because we are his posterity; and we are his posterity because he begot us; and he begot us insofar as he begot Seth. Therefore the act by which he begot Seth precedes the imputation of sin in the order of nature. And yet, if the learned man is believed, Adam's sin was imputed to us long before he had begotten Seth, at the very time it was committed: either then it also preceded Adam's coming to be.
317: GAR. Sixth it is asked. If as Christ's righteousness is imputed to us, so also Adam's sin is ours by imputation, why is Adam not called our sin as Christ is called our righteousness? Reply 1. That God speaks as He wills; that it is ours to be content with those phrases which occur in the Scriptures, and which set forth God's mind, so far as our salvation is concerned, clearly enough. Although therefore Scripture does not say Adam is our sin, yet it uses those locutions which manifestly mark imputation, of which enough was said before. PLAC. I do not remember using this reason or interrogation, nor do I know whose it is: yet whether mine or another's, it seems fitted to refute the major of the argument on which immediate imputation usually most leans—As we are constituted righteous through Christ, in the same way we were constituted sinners through Adam: for it shows a memorable difference between Christ and Adam.
